pairs.question: Quis potis est dignum pollenti pectore carmen condere pro rerum maiestate hisque repertis? quisve valet verbis tantum, qui fingere laudes pro meritis eius possit, qui talia nobis pectore parta suo quaesitaque praemia liquit?
pairs.answer: nemo, ut opinor, erit mortali corpore cretus.
pairs.derivation: Didactic verse; authorial-rhetorical. The poet poses a genuine double interrogative (lines 3-7: 'Who can compose a worthy poem... or who is strong enough in words to fashion praises worthy of his merits?') and answers it himself in line 8 with 'nemo, ut opinor, erit mortali corpore cretus' ('no one, I think, will be born of mortal body'). Answer window stops at the first full stop after 'cretus'; the following 'nam si...' (line 9) begins elaboration on why Epicurus deserves to be called a god, which no longer answers the 'who can?' question. No scaffolding (no section markers, verse numbers, or footer) fell inside either span; the title line (1) and trailing footer (1462) are outside. Other interrogatives in the book (e.g. the Hercules-labors questions 26-40, 'quidve mali fuerat nobis non esse creatis' 176, 'saltu pernici... quid potis est' 561-562) are rhetorical questions woven into ongoing argument with no clean, contiguous answering span, so they are dropped per the false-negative preference.
